methodological_rigor.justification: The study tests five isolated compounds on two breast cancer cell lines using MTT, CCK-8, colony formation and wound-healing assays supplemented with in silico docking and ADME prediction, but the design has important methodological gaps. No IC50 values are reported, positive chemotherapeutic controls (e.g., doxorubicin was only used in docking, not in vitro) are missing in the cellular assays, no normal/non-malignant cell line is included to assess selectivity, and the docking 're-validation' claims identical RMSD/binding energy (0.70 A and -14.41 kcal/mol) for two different targets, suggesting a copy-paste error that was not caught. Statistical analysis relied on ANOVA with Dunnett's post hoc in triplicate only, with no power calculation, effect sizes, or confidence intervals reported; some figure captions mention concentrations (10 and 20 ug/mL) that differ from those described in the methods text (15 and 30 ug/mL), raising internal consistency concerns.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is an entirely preclinical in vitro and in silico study on two immortalized breast cancer cell lines with molecular docking and ADME prediction, mapping to Oxford LoE 5 (mechanistic/basic science). The translational path is speculative: the most active compound TM36 has low predicted GI absorption, violates multiple drug-likeness filters, and carries a BRENK alert, which the authors themselves acknowledge. No animal data, no pharmacodynamic validation, and no selectivity versus non-cancerous cells are provided, limiting near-term clinical relevance.

reporting_quality.justification: No reporting-standard checklist is declared; the closest applicable preclinical framework would be ARRIVE-like standards for in vitro experimentation, but key items (blinding, randomization of wells, sample-size justification, exact replicate numbers per condition) are missing. Figure captions are inconsistent with the methods section regarding concentrations and timepoints, and raw NMR and docking outputs are relegated to unseen supplementary files. Data availability is limited: there is no deposition of raw data, no code/scripts for docking parameters beyond citing a prior paper, and supplementary tables are referenced but not independently accessible in-text, so reproducibility is weak.

novelty_literature.justification: The compounds studied (terminolic acid, arjungenin, arjunglucoside I, 24-deoxysericoside, chebuloside II) are known oleanane-type triterpenoids/saponins, and the authors' own prior work (reference 24) already reported their isolation and anticholinesterase/antidiabetic testing. Extending these compounds to MCF-7 and MDA-MB-231 cytotoxicity with docking into hERalpha and PI3Kalpha is an incremental application of a well-established workflow, and the discussion itself cites multiple prior reports that saponins and oleanane triterpenoids inhibit breast cancer cell lines. Novelty is therefore limited to the specific compound-target pairing rather than a new mechanism or scaffold.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is generally readable but contains numerous typographical and grammatical issues ('Breastcancer', 'Futureperspectives', 'Effects Deoxysericoside', 'E8 or DMSO'), inconsistent abbreviation usage, and several internal contradictions (e.g., colony-formation doses described as 15/30 ug/mL in text but 10/20 ug/mL in Figure 4 caption; migration doses described variably as 10/20 and 15/30 ug/mL). The structure is conventional but the results section repeats methodological detail, and the discussion is largely a catalog of prior literature rather than focused interpretation of the new findings.

key_strengths: Combines in vitro cytotoxicity (MTT, CCK-8), colony formation, and wound healing with molecular docking and SwissADME predictions into a coherent screening workflow.
Identifies 24-deoxysericoside (TM36) as the most active compound with reproducible, dose-dependent effects in MDA-MB-231 cells at 15 and 30 ug/mL.
Discusses structure-activity relationships around glycosylation and the 24-OH group, providing some mechanistic framing.
key_concerns: No IC50 values, no positive in vitro chemotherapeutic control, and no non-malignant cell line to assess selectivity, undermining interpretation of the cytotoxicity data.
Docking validation reports identical RMSD (0.70 A) and binding energy (-14.41 kcal/mol) for two different targets (hERalpha and PI3Kalpha), strongly suggestive of a copy-paste/reporting error.
Internal inconsistencies between methods text and figure captions regarding tested concentrations (10/20 vs 15/30 ug/mL) and timepoints for colony formation and migration assays.

TM36 has poor predicted oral bioavailability (0.17), low GI absorption, multiple drug-likeness filter violations, and a BRENK structural alert, which are acknowledged but not addressed in the translational claims.
Reporting is weak: no ARRIVE-style checklist, no blinding/randomization, no power calculation, experiments in triplicate only with no effect sizes or confidence intervals.
Novelty is limited: compounds were previously isolated and characterized by the same group, and saponin/triterpenoid cytotoxicity against MCF-7/MDA-MB-231 is well documented.
chief_reviewer.rationale: The manuscript is a competent but incremental preclinical natural-product screen with notable methodological and reporting weaknesses (missing IC50s, selectivity controls, internal inconsistencies, and a suspicious duplicated docking-validation statistic). It is most plausibly a Tier 4 journal candidate and would need major revisions to address controls, inconsistencies, and translational caveats before acceptance.
